lede: Magic & Ritual · ไสยศาสตร์ accounts for 276 catalogued manuscripts, 276 of them flagged research-priority. It clusters in Nan (42% of the corpus for this genre), ahead of Phayao and Lampang. Nearly all (94%) are written in Tham Lanna · อักษรธรรมล้านนา script. By support it leans to mulberry paper (saa) · กระดาษสา (51%) over palm-leaf · ใบลาน (42%). Dated witnesses run 1622–1988 CE (53 of 276 carry a date).

authored.body_html:
What this is

Saiyasat (ไสยศาสตร์) is the science of making something happen — the efficacious half of northern religion. Its instruments are the nyan (the drawn diagram), the katha (the spoken formula), and the consecration — pluk sek, phutthaphisek — that turns an inert object or an ordinary morning into something that works. It is the esoteric core this archive exists to document, and every one of its 276 witnesses is flagged research-priority.

This is also the page where the archive's two halves meet and refuse to reconcile politely. On one side sits the Lanna palm-leaf and folding-paper shelf, whose titles are overwhelmingly benedictory: rice-offerings, robe-consecrations, life-extensions, soul-callings. On the other sit fourteen contributed printed treatises whose pages are transcribed and translated in full — and those pages will tell you which day to forge a knife out of iron robbed from seven cremation grounds. Both are saiyasat. The rest of this page is about how that is possible.

The story, first — a boy, a mantra, and a gun that burst

The best account of how this knowledge actually moves between people is told in the first person, by a man remembering himself at eight years old, in Mind Stream — Key to Saiyasat (p.36–38).

Three of his father's students walk in from Ban On Nuea, in Pak Phanang district, each carrying an air rifle. The narrator explains why, flatly: tigers were fierce there and bandits plentiful, so every house kept a gun and you carried it wherever you went. The three men hunt together, so naturally they come to study together. They have already passed through the invulnerability branch; this time they want maha-ut — the charm that stops a gun from firing. The father teaches it, and attaches one prohibition, which he states twice: never cover a gun barrel with your hand — not your own, not a friend's — because if you hold your breath and recite over a covered muzzle, the gun will not fire out of the muzzle. It will burst instead.

The boy is asleep in the same room. At dawn the three men go out to wash their faces, and he wakes up alone with their rifles propped against the wall. So he does what any eight-year-old would do with a brand-new piece of forbidden knowledge. He holds his breath, presses his palm over the muzzle of Mr Saeng's gun, and recites — na ut mo ut na mo phutthaya dtantani — for several held breaths. The men come back in, collect their guns, and go home.

Three months later Mr Saeng returns with a new gun and a grievance. Five days after getting home he had chased a wounded deer, fired, and the barrel had split open in the middle. He is certain Mr Nuan did it, and he says out loud what a man says out loud in that world: had it been anyone but a fellow disciple of the same teacher, he would have had to shoot him dead. Mr Nuan comes and denies it. Then the father turns to his son.

The interrogation that follows is the whole ethical structure of the tradition compressed into six questions. Have you memorised the maha-ut mantra? — I have. Recite it. — he recites it. How is it done? — hold the breath and chant with the palm on the navel, every day before sleeping. What is forbidden? — to press the hand on the muzzle of your own gun or anyone else's. Did you do it to Saeng's gun? — once. And then the verdict, which is not about the gun: do you know that doing such a thing is called breaking an instruction? From now on, never break an instruction again.

The writer's own moral is stranger than the story. He tells it, he says, to show that even the most foolish person — a child who could not yet write a single letter and knew only the namo — got a result, because he had no doubt whatsoever. The middling student, half-learned, fails; the treatise's word for what ruins him is vicikicchā, canonical Buddhist doubt (p.36). Inference — the tradition's own theory of failure is not that the formula is weak. It is that the practitioner is divided. That is why so much of what follows is discipline rather than recipe.

What the shelf actually tells you to do

The treatises are not shy. Making Sacred Charms and Amulets announces its own scale on p.22: 42 kinds of amulet-making manual and 158 different forms, indexed like a parts catalogue — Nang Kwak, Hanuman, the tiger-fang, the wua thanu bull-of-the-bow, the palad khik, the stillborn-child luk krok, the ritual knife, the Kuman Thong, boiled love-charm oil, boiled magic lip-wax, a rattan rod for subduing spirits, a figure of a lersi to be moulded.

Three entries are worth reading as procedure, because procedure is where the audacity lives.

The ritual knife (mid mo, p.86–88) begins as metallurgy with a grudge. The smith is to gather ten irons and forge them into one blade: iron from a stupa finial, from a prang tower, from a prasat spire, kamchat and kamchai iron, "good" iron, Nam Phi iron, shrimp-tail iron, palace-gate iron — and iron from seven cremation grounds. While he works he keeps the five or eight precepts; the forging is done on a Saturday and a Tuesday, with vegetarian offerings and bai si trays set to left and right and monks chanting the karaniya seven times. Finished, the blade is quenched three times and seven times in prai-oil. The handle is then loaded with powder ground from the foreheads of four bad deaths — one who died in childbirth, one drowned, one hanged, one struck by lightning — mixed with flower-tips and medicinal powder, each katha recited over it 108 times. The claimed effects escalate calmly: scratch a line on the ground and the enemy stops there; plant the knife at a crevice and everyone sleeps; even an invulnerable man can be cut by it. And then, quietly, the condition on the whole apparatus: hold to truthfulness and it is efficacious. The knife succeeds by force of mind. The second method (p.88) supplies the awakening chant, a rolling cosmological boast that names every foreign iron it intends to command — Indian, Hollander, English, Khom, Cham-China, Brahmin-Lawa, Burma, Mon-Mataban, Lao and Karen — a Southeast Asian arms inventory rendered as liturgy.

The Kuman Thong (p.91, p.94–95) is the passage the market never stopped citing, and it is smaller and sadder than its reputation. The practitioner is directed to a child who died tai thang klom, whole — mother and infant together — or one who died while the mother was still in post-partum confinement on the kradan fai, the fire-board; best on a Saturday or a Tuesday. You go to fetch it with a candle at the head and a candle at the feet, two krathong trays of spicy shrimp and fish salad, two bananas. You explain yourself to the child: father will take you to raise as his son. You tell it where the house is, so it can find its way. And then the text remembers one more party and turns startlingly courteous — inform the mae sü, the spirit-mother who took the child to raise as her own, "because we are going to ask for it" (p.95). A negotiation with the dead conducted according to the etiquette of adoption. The same page's practical register is the household's: feed it rice daily, wake it before it eats, bind it closed with a katha before you put it away. Read this beside Khun Phaen, whose epic supplies the practice's origin story, and beside the archive's own Hun Payont — the animated servant-figure is the same idea with the grief taken out.

The tiger-fang (p.77–78) starts as carving — a crouching tiger, a seated tiger, a leaping tiger, cut from a real fang, steeped in scented oil — and then opens into the single strangest page in the corpus. The awakening chant becomes a roll-call, and what it calls is a company of named women: Mae-nang Et, Mae-nang Sai, Mae-nang Chop, Mae-nang Phueak, Mae-nang Hongsa who veils her husband's eyes, Mae-nang Saem who steeps a hundred pots of medicine to make the light of a beloved man. Thirty deities are summoned to hold the reciter's arms and lead the van, forty to hold his arms and guard the rear, "according to the day's strength." Then the register drops from cosmic to intimate without a seam: come and stay at the belly, come and stay in the lap; cling to the shin and do not slip. Inference — the fang is nominally a warrior's charm, but its consecration is a love-charm wearing armour, and the seam between the two is invisible because in this tradition there is no seam — kong kraphan and saneh run on one engine.

The rules — a discipline before it is a repertoire

Every treatise that gives a method also gives the fence around it, and the fences are more revealing than the methods.

  • Three prohibitions on the invulnerability craft (Teaching Meditation and Psychic Power, p.27). One: do not pass the formula on — five full years of study, or a teacher-raising ceremony first. Two: do not use paper bearing Thai or Khom script to wipe yourself. Three: do not curse someone's mother in a fight. A transmission rule, a script-reverence rule, and a temper rule, ranked together as equals.
  • A weekday diet. The Life of Luang Por Thob (p.50) forbids a food to each birth-weekday: water spinach for those born on Sunday, coriander for Monday, pickled cleome for Tuesday, boiled aubergine for Wednesday, pork for Thursday, phak bang for Friday, moringa leaves for Saturday. Break it and the charm will not take; keep it and your amulets will outperform other people's. Inference — this is horā operating inside saiyasat: the birth-day that sets your fate in the astrologer's table also sets what you may eat, and efficacy is made to depend on the calendar the diviner keeps.
  • The blind yantra. Yantra Inscription Formulas in Mixed Khom and Thai (p.42) sets the drafting rule and the failure state in one breath: the line must be drawn in a single continuous stroke, finishing exactly as the formula finishes, because stopping partway is spoiled. And the one absolute prohibition — no character or numeral may ever cross a line of the diagram. Such a yantra is called a blind yantra and cannot be used. The same page explains why the script is Khom, and why the yantra compartments are so often filled with bare numerals: a number stands in for a formula too long to write, so the numeral 7 in a cell means the heart-formula of the seven books of the Abhidhamma. The 108 Na are the same compression, one glyph further down.
  • What it costs. Yantra Craft and Katha of the Lanna Lineage (p.71) prices a working. White flowers, incense, candles, scented water, perfumed water, a bottle of Mekhong rum and a bottle of foreign liquor, all into one basin — and a minimum teacher's fee of 998 baht. Best performed at a cremation pyre; next best a graveyard; at home if you must. Three times in full. Then three prohibitions again, one of them the drying-rail rule that also appears in the corpus's oldest conduct list.
  • The conduct list itself. Compendium of Katha from Old Manuals (p.15–16) does something unexpected: rather than invent house rules, it reprints Sawatdirak, the didactic verse attributed to Sunthorn Phu, as the standing daily observance for anyone studying spells. Face east at sunrise and east again when eating; north brings ill fortune and loss of life. Cut your nails on Wednesday and Monday. Bathe facing downstream, never up. Never step over amulets, tattooed cords, or weapons. Do not pass beneath a bridge, a house beam, or a fence rail, "so that the power of one's spells will remain potent." And a wardrobe keyed to the week — creamy white on Monday, purple with indigo on Tuesday, orange on Wednesday, green on Thursday, storm-cloud grey on Friday for going to war, black on Saturday, best of all.

Demonstrations, and a man who took a sword to another man's arm

Two treatises put the claims where they can be checked, and both are more uncomfortable than a sceptic expects.

Akhom Magic of Phra Narai opens by sorting the whole field into two categories — the kind that helps its user, and the kind that helps its user by wrecking someone else (p.15). Its account of the second category is unsparing: burying a carved effigy of an enemy near his house; plòi khun, enchanting a strip of flesh or hide until it can walk and releasing it into the air to enter whoever it meets, fatal if it cannot be countered; twisting the entrails by binding. "We who are Buddhists should never engage in using mantras wrongly in this way" (p.18). Then, having condemned the misuse, the author testifies for the defence — and the testimony is the passage that will not leave you. A man who had finished his chant held out his arm to be struck. The author picked up a very sharp sword and struck down at the base of the arm with full force, and admits in the same sentence that he did not stop to think what would follow if he took the man's arm off. There was a mark like a thorn-scratch and blood oozing drop by drop. Even so, he closes, he still cannot say for certain whether the man was truly invulnerable or whether the blade failed for some other reason (p.17). Inference — the archive's own sceptical apparatus is inside the tradition, not outside it.

Training the Power of the Mind, vol. 2 does the same in public and keeps a diary of it (p.164–166). The author lists his demonstrations by date and venue: the Signal Corps Regiment at Bang Sue in December 1954; the Psychiatric Association and then the Buddhist Association at Wat Bowon in March 1956; television, Channel 4, on 15 April 1956; the Astrologers' Association of Thailand that September; the Phim Thai newspaper at his own house in 1957; Channel 7 in 1960, that time taking mercury in through the palm and calling it back out. The standard programme is three feats — gripping a chain heated red-hot, plunging a hand into boiling coconut oil and scooping some out to eat, and Mr Yu jumping from a table onto broken glass and rolling on it — with the audience invited to try. Then the Cold War walks in. A delegation of five foreign representatives from a SEATO meeting, September 1960; an American Air Force engineering officer from Don Mueang who asked to test invulnerability at the house; and on 28 September 1962, the Army Education Department's hall, with the head of JUSMAG present and an American counter-guerrilla training team — where Lieutenant Colonel Brown, head of the American training team, put his own hand into the boiling oil and was also stabbed in the arm. The same volume elsewhere reframes the whole craft as medicine: mind-power is for treating illness, "such as treating wounds by releasing the power of invulnerability" (p.97). And Teaching Meditation and Psychic Power teaches the technique as a curriculum with a testing protocol — consecrated lime paste touched to the side of the neck on a held breath (p.20), the test scheduled at least a day apart from the consecration so no doubt muddies the result (p.25), a variant for making war elephants and horses invulnerable by smearing the lime on the animal's neck (p.28) — and insists throughout that the operator first make the mind loving toward every person alive (p.23).

What the Lanna shelf holds

Now turn to the palm-leaf and folding-paper catalogue, and the register changes completely.

Ritual is emphatically a Nan genre. Of the 276 witnesses, 115 are from Nan — more than the next three muang combined (Phayao 36, Lampang 29, Phrae 26), with Chiang Mai at 18 and Chiang Rai at 11. Three Nan temples carry the weight, and the archive's own findings already flag them as the most magic-dense shelves in the collection: Wat Si Mongkhon (Kong) and Wat Pa Mueat with 30 apiece and Wat Hia with 23. Almost all of it is Tham Lanna (259 of 276) in the mixed Pali-and-Lan Na register. Its physical support splits nearly evenly — 140 mulberry-paper phap sa against 117 palm-leaf — where astrology leans hard toward paper. Inference — the consecration and offering texts were copied into the durable canonical format alongside the liturgy they accompany, while the working almanac was not; the split is a fossil of two different kinds of use.

109 of the 276 have no title at all, and 44 of those are catalogued only by what the cataloguer could see inside — nyan and/or katha — a bundle of diagrams and formulae with no name on the cover. This is the same lesson the paṭiloma page teaches: this register lives at section level, below the resolution of a title search. Across the genre, 55 titles name a katha, 29 name a nyan, and 16 name both in one breath — nyan lae khatha, over and over, the drawn and the spoken filed as one object.

The titles that do speak describe a working ritualist's year, and they are concrete to the point of bluntness:

  • Consecration. Putthaphisek (พุทธาภิเสก), the rite that makes an image a Buddha, is the genre's deepest root — 10 witnesses here and 15 across the corpus, and the earliest dated manuscript in this genre by well over a century: ms 4580, dated 1622, at Wat Lai Hin Luang in Lampang — the next-oldest dated witness in the genre is 1766. Alongside it sits ms 522 from Wat Pa Mueat, whose contents include คำไขตาพระเจ้า — the words for opening the Lord's eyes.
  • Un-doing. 17 titles name a thon and four name khuet, the Lanna taboo-pollution: ms 220 at Wat Phra That Chang Kham binds together the withdrawal of a death-spirit, of all khuet, of disease, and of everyone who died a tai hong death; ms 490 at Wat Pa Mueat includes a recitation to un-do a charnel ground. The thon page follows this thread.
  • Calling and extending. 32 titles name a khwan and 12 a suep cata, often together — ms 423 at Wat Hia pairs a grandmother's soul-calling with a life-extension. The rice gets both (ms 328, ms 333, ms 450); so does the buffalo (ms 319, ms 530), and so does an elephant (ms 538 at Wat Pa Mueat, bound with elephant-physiognomy, a Tai Yuan primer, and holasat). See su khwan and suep cata, and the archive's own living su khwan for machines.
  • Brushing and sending. ms 322 gives a method for brushing away forest-spirits; ms 323 for brushing cattle and brushing danger; ms 545 for sending off the misfortune of a house fire; ms 511 includes the binding of an infant's wrists.
  • Feeding and giving. Rice-offering verses run right through — puca khao pha mueang kaeo, kham thwai khao mathupayat, the 49 rice-balls (ms 86, ms 372) — plus eight wen tan dedications and the ongkalakkhana of a mahakathin robe (ms 45, Wat Phra Sing, 1849).

Inference — nothing on the Lanna shelf is a printed treatise's catalogue of charms, and nothing in the printed treatises is a village's offering calendar; but the same technology runs both. The formula is recited over the rice and over the knife alike. The catalogue's raw label for 262 of these — a single undifferentiated Custom / Ritual — is what happens when a metadata scheme meets a science it has no column for.

Handling this material

This archive treats esoteric material descriptively. The catalogue and these articles record the existence, provenance and shape of a rite; where a contributed treatise is already a published book, we summarise what its page says and cite the page so a reader can check us. We do not present this as an instruction manual, we do not reproduce untranslated activation formulae as though handing them over, and material a lineage would treat as khong khru (restricted teacher-knowledge) is described only at the level a public finding-aid needs. The treatises themselves are stricter than we are, and say so on the page — see the transmission rule at Teaching Meditation and Psychic Power p.27. Takedown and correction requests go to 530kings@proton.me.

Notes

  • The bucket is coarse. 262 of the 276 arrived under one raw label, Custom / Ritual, so real distinctions — consecration, offering, protective, un-doing, life-extension, soul-calling — are collapsed. Splitting this into sub-genres is the obvious next taxonomy pass, and the title evidence for the split is already sitting in the counts above.
  • Where to go next. Browse the genre to see the 276 in provenance order; find by need approaches the same material from the other end, by what a person came wanting; what it is made of tracks the material axis — prai, bone, metal, herb — that the amulet manuals above spend most of their pages on; and the glossary holds the emic vocabulary these titles use.
  • Read it with its neighbours. Astrology supplies the day, the hour and the direction that nearly every rite here depends on; liturgy and chanting is the same technology performed in public, in the vihara, by monks. Where a title names both a holasat and a katha, the object is a household manual and the genre line is only recording which half won.
  • A crawl and transcription priority. The 44 untitled nyan-and-katha bundles are the highest-value unread material in the collection. The printed treatises give the search image: look for the single-stroke inscription rule, the weekday food prohibition, the 108-times consecration count, and the numeral standing in for a heart-formula. Anything that surfaces a named na or a named yant under a Nan or Lampang hand is a finding.
